summary: A note on experiences implementing Network Graphics Protocol Level 0 at several hosts, with the remote host acting as the last intelligent machine before a Computek display. It aims to clarify the coordinate system and puzzles over how to handle text strings. An appendix outlines converting coordinates.

eli5.summary: People trying out a drawing protocol share what confused them, like how to measure positions on the screen and where to put text.

subtitle: Implementers of Network Graphics Protocol Level 0 ask how coordinates are encoded and how to handle text strings.

tldr.problem: The NGP-0 document did not say whether absolute and relative coordinates share one number format, and the TEXTR command needs the beam position afterwards although Level 0 is meant to keep no state.
tldr.mechanism: The authors propose one two's complement fraction format (System B, range -1 to +1 - 2^-15) for both kinds of coordinate, and track the beam with software X and Y registers.
tldr.outcome: They will use these choices in all their implementations, and an appendix shows how to convert NGP-0 fractions to PDP-10 floating point. RFC 401 is listed as updating this note.

today: The metadata lists no formal status for RFC 387, and it says the note is updated by RFC 401. It records implementation experience with NGP-0 as defined in RFC 292.

sections.title: Implementing NGP-0 for a Computek Display
sections.content:
The authors are implementing Network Graphics Protocol Level 0 (NGP-0, defined in RFC 292) at several hosts. For now they treat the remote host as the last intelligent machine, and they translate NGP-0 into a machine dependent code for the Computek display. The remote hosts are CCN, UCSD and soon RANDCSG.

This RFC has two concerns: clarifying the coordinate number system, and working out how to handle the TEXTR string command. More comments are promised in later RFCs.
sections.eli5: A few teams are building the same drawing helper for a particular screen. This note is about two things that puzzled them.

sections.title: The Coordinate Data
sections.content:
RFC 292 does not say that coordinate data has the same format in absolute and relative mode. It says only that coordinates are in two's complement with the leftmost bit as the sign bit. That allows two readings. System A for absolute coordinates has range -1/2 to +1/2 - 2^-16, never hands you an out-of-range number and has one more bit of precision. System B for relative coordinates has range -1 to +1 - 2^-15.

The authors argue that two systems cloud the issue and need extra coding. System B for both handles absolute and relative coordinates with a single system, wraps around neatly if an absolute coordinate exceeds range (just force the sign bit on), and matches the mantissa of floating point numbers on most machines. They will use System B for both in all their implementations unless shown overwhelming contrary logic.
sections.eli5: There were two ways to write down a spot on the screen as a number. The authors say to pick just one way for everything, so the programs stay simple.

sections.title: The TEXTR Command and Beam Position
sections.content:
RFC 292 asks that a command be included only if its output depends solely on the current command and the beam position at its start, so a Level 0 interpreter needs no stored modes or stacks. On the Computek display most NGP commands match device capabilities. The exception is TEXTR, which needs to know what beam position to return to after the string is drawn.

Reading the cursor position from the device is not possible until input protocols exist, and it is accurate only to within 4 scope points. So the implementations monitor beam motion in software with an X register and a Y register. Absolute commands set them, relative commands add to them, and both are set to 0 at the beginning and end of a picture. TEXTR also increments X for each character.
sections.eli5: To write words and then go back to where you were, you must remember your spot. The screen cannot tell you, so the program keeps its own note of where the pen is.

sections.title: Appendix: Conversion to PDP-10 Floating Point
sections.content:
NGP-0 treats X and Y values as 16-bit fractions with the binary point between bits 0 and 1, bit 0 being the sign bit. The PDP-10 floating point mantissa is very similar, except for the number -1, so the conversion takes three steps: move the sign bit, move the 15 fraction bits left justified into the mantissa, and fill in the 8-bit exponent. Positive numbers get exponent 80 hex and negative numbers 7F hex. The one exception is -1 in NGP, whose mantissa becomes the same as -1/2 and whose exponent is 7D hex.

The method stays the same for up to 24 bits of NGP fraction.
sections.eli5: The appendix is a recipe for turning the drawing numbers into the form one particular computer likes, with a single special case.
